catalog_quote: Las Casas is usually very careful to indicate which syllable bears strong stress, and Oviedo frequently does so as well. For this reason it is possible to say that stress itself does not seem to have been phonemic in Taíno. Generally speaking, the chroniclers wrote Taíno words and used the acute accent (') to stress syllables which did not abide by the Spanish rules of accentuation - last syllable if the word ended in a consonant other than n or s, the next to last syllable if the word ended in a vowel, with exceptions indicated by the acute accent mark. From these orthographic rules, it seems evident that primary stress normally fell on the next to last syllable, but on the final syllable of a multisyllabic word which ended in [e], [i], or one of the nasalized vowels, as in Manatí, burén ('griddle'), Maniabón. new_statements.rule_in_words: Inferred from chroniclers' Spanish accent-marking: stress non-phonemic; default on the penultimate syllable, but word-final when a polysyllable ends in e, i, or a nasalized vowel (Manatí, burén, Maniabón); final orthographic <x> may also signal final stress. Authors flag the inference as 'admittedly problematic'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress (a search for 'secondary stress' in the volume returned no Taíno hit).
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress in polysyllables ending in [e], [i] or a nasalized vowel; possible final stress marked by orthographic final <x> (=[h]?); monosyllables aside. Whole analysis rests on Las Casas's and Oviedo's acute-accent usage relative to 16th-c. Spanish accentuation rules.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, philological reconstruction from colonial orthography (citation forms of nouns/toponyms as written by Las Casas, Oviedo, etc.); no phrase-level data exist. Quote is verbatim but assembled from overlapping Google Books snippets, not from a page image — continuity at the junctions is secured by multi-word overlaps; paragraphing/italics unknown.
new_statements.identity_note: Granberry & Vescelius describe 'Classic Taíno' (the Hispaniola/eastern Cuba/Puerto Rico prestige variety recorded by Las Casas, Oviedo, Pané, Pedro Mártir) = Glottolog tain1254 / ISO tnq; they treat Ciboney Taíno, Macorís and Ciguayo separately (the p. 27 snippet is from the chapter on non-Taíno 'anomalous' data). The stress statement is a philological inference from 16th-c. Spanish accent-marking, not from speech.
